core: Social control as the regulation and enforcement of norms (working definition, attributed)
Internal vs external social control (self-regulation vs outside pressure)
Informal vs formal sanctions (reactions from people vs systems; laws and police as formal control)
Positive and negative sanctions, each with an example
Socialization as the route by which control becomes internal (one line; sibling topic)
Honest note: control can overreach (factual, no policy position)
Honest framing: social control as the gravity of social life
supporting: Social order as the goal of social control
Internalization of norms (guilt/shame, no external sanctions needed)
Conformity even when authority figures are absent
outOfScope: Deviance and deviance theories (sibling topic sociology:foundations:deviance)
Crime and the criminal justice system (sibling topic sociology:foundations:crime-and-society)
Legal systems and legal doctrine (owned by the law subject)

claims.claim: Social control is the regulation and enforcement of norms, and its underlying goal is to maintain social order (an arrangement of practices and behaviors on which society's members base their daily lives).
All societies practice social control, and it operates even when authority figures such as law enforcement are not present.
Sanctions — rewards and punishments — are the means by which norms are enforced.
Positive sanctions are rewards given for conforming to norms (praise, bonuses, commendations); negative sanctions are punishments for violating norms (frowns, fines, suspensions).
Informal sanctions arise in face-to-face interactions, while formal sanctions are officially recognized and enforced by organizations; laws and police sit at the formal end of social control.

Through socialization people internalize norms, so that conformity comes from within — people feel guilt or shame at the prospect of violating norms, and external sanctions are not always needed once internalization succeeds.
Socialization, beginning in infancy, is the process through which people learn and internalize the norms that become internal social control.
Formal social control can be applied unevenly and can criminalize behavior that most people do not consider harmful; this is presented as a factual observation, not a policy position.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Texts differ in emphasis on whether social control is defined by its goal (maintaining order) or by its mechanisms (sanctions and conformity).
positions: OpenStax 7.1 defines social control as the regulation and enforcement of norms, with the underlying goal of maintaining social order
OpenStax 3.2 describes sanctions as a form of social control and emphasizes encouraging conformity to cultural norms or rules
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the OpenStax working definition (regulation and enforcement of norms) as primary and treats sanctions as the means of enforcement, which both sections support.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The explicit 'internal vs external social control' terminology is not used verbatim in OpenStax 3e section 7.1.
positions: Internal control = self-regulation through internalized norms, with guilt or shame at the prospect of violation (SEP, Social Norms, on internalization)
External control = pressure from outside the person via sanctions and authority (OpenStax on sanctions and on conformity when authority figures are absent)
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the internal/external contrast as a standard sociological distinction, supported by SEP on internalization and by OpenStax on sanctions and authority-independent conformity; it does not claim OpenStax 7.1 uses the exact terms.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The machine-generated draft described social control only as 'a foundational concept in Sociology' with no definition, mechanisms, or examples; no definitional or factual content from the draft survived research.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the generic draft with the OpenStax working definition (regulation and enforcement of norms), the internal/external and informal/formal distinctions, and the four sanction types, all verified against sources.
Added the honest note on uneven enforcement and overreach as an attributed observation (OpenStax 7.1 gambling example), explicitly framed as description rather than policy.
Clarified that laws and police are one formal instrument of social control, not the whole concept, and that legal systems belong to the law subject.
rightsIssues: OpenStax Introduction to Sociology 3e is CC BY 4.0; used as reference only, with short attributed definitions and no adapted prose.
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy 'Social Norms' entry used as reference only; only brief attributed phrases quoted.

sourceRecords.title: 3.2 Elements of Culture — Introduction to Sociology 3e
sourceRecords.notes: Supports: sanctions as a form of social control (ways to encourage conformity to norms); positive sanctions (e.g., good grades bringing praise) and negative sanctions (frowns, scoldings; traffic tickets, fines, imprisonment); the point that social control leads most people to conform regardless of whether authority figures such as law enforcement are present. Read via Internet Archive capture of the canonical openstax.org URL (2026-08-22).

sourceRecords.title: 7.1 Deviance and Control — Introduction to Sociology 3e
sourceRecords.notes: Supports: the working definition of social control (the regulation and enforcement of norms); the goal of maintaining social order; the claim that all societies practice social control; sanctions as the means of enforcing rules; positive sanctions (rewards for conforming) and negative sanctions (punishments for violating); informal sanctions emerging in face-to-face interactions vs formal sanctions officially recognizing and enforcing norm violations (expulsion, firing, arrest, official commendation); the decades-old gambling example showing a generally non-deviant behavior made criminal (control can overreach); the observation that deviance does not always align with punishment. Read via Internet Archive capture of the canonical openstax.org URL (2026-08-22).

sourceRecords.title: Ch. 7 Key Terms — Introduction to Sociology 3e
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the lesson's vocabulary definitions: social control (the regulation and enforcement of norms), social order (an arrangement of practices and behaviors on which society's members base their daily lives), formal sanctions (officially recognized and enforced), informal sanctions (occur in face-to-face interactions), positive sanctions (rewards given for conforming to norms), negative sanctions (punishments for violating norms), and legal codes (codes that maintain formal social control through laws). Read via Internet Archive capture of the canonical openstax.org URL (2026-08-22).

sourceRecords.title: Social Norms (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
sourceRecords.notes: Supports: internalization as the process by which people develop a motive to conform to shared norms; that internalization proceeds through socialization beginning in infancy; that when norms are internalized people typically feel guilt or shame at the prospect of behaving in a deviant way; and that if internalization succeeds external sanctions play no role in eliciting conformity — the basis for the lesson's internal vs external control distinction and the socialization-as-control line. Read directly at plato.stanford.edu (2026-08-22).
